case_data.title: Global AI Dialogues
case_data.provide-a-brief-description-of-the-proje:
In 2024, the Technical University of Munich initiated a process that used participatory futures workshops and surveys to involve approximately 284 people in one-day dialogue workshops.

The Global AI Dialogues are a dialogue series that invites citizens around the world to engage, discuss, and contribute their perspectives on the topic of Artificial Intelligence (AI), specifically generative AI and facial processing technologies. So far, the dialogues have taken place in Bolivia, Mexico, Nigeria, India, Germany, and Japan. 

During the one-day dialogue workshop, participants explore the deployment of technology in specific contexts, reflect on its future implications for societies, determine whether they consider its future deployment desirable, and identify relevant measures to support its desirable deployment – or alternative measures in the event that its deployment is not deemed desirable. In addition to providing spaces for discourse, the Global AI Dialogues is an international research project comparing participants’ perspectives cross-nationally.
case_data.what-limitations-to-the-project-should-b:
One limitation of conducting dialogues is the necessary budget for participant compensation, food and drinks, and venue costs. This restricts either the number of participants per location or the number of locations where the dialogues can be held. For the Global AI Dialogues, for example, our financial resources limited the dialogues to six countries. 

For our multi-location dialogues, all implementing research teams applied the same sampling criteria and attempted to achieve demographic heterogeneity through targeted sampling. Given different age structures, university quotas, and factors such as familiarity and openness to participating in dialogues, the samples in the six countries are inevitably different from each other. Our priority was to apply the same sampling criteria and achieve a sample that resembled the location of the dialogue. We acknowledge that our sample ended up being rather educated.

In terms of methodology, the Global AI Dialogues feature a participatory futuring workshop paired with individual surveys conducted at specific points in time: before, during, and after the dialogues. During the dialogues, we use design futuring approaches to facilitate conversations about AI. We prompt participants to consider future AI deployment, which sets the stage for collective exploration. Participants imagine and evaluate potential consequences based on their experiences and viewpoints. They also explore the roles and interests of the involved stakeholders. The guided process results in a set of measures for different actors to pursue in order to support the desirable deployment or non-deployment of AI in the discussed application context. As a multi-country research project, the Global AI Dialogues enable comparative analysis of the results. This analysis was performed by an international research team, composed of the researchers who organized and facilitated the local dialogues, through joint analysis workshops.
case_data.headline-findings:
The results from the dialogues were jointly analyzed by an international research team, composed of the researchers who organized and facilitated the local dialogues. The reported findings reflect the researchers’ synthesis.

For future usage of generative AI (genAI) systems, laypeople in Nigeria, Japan, and Germany envisioned the future value of these systems in educational, public service, and artistic contexts to make valuable goods (knowledge, public service, and art creation) more accessible to everyone, thus making them public goods. People expressed specific requirements that must be met in order for the envisioned value to be realized. These requirements include, among others, mindful regulation, technical robustness, and a knowledgeable population with broad access to the technology. 

For future usage of facial processing technology, laypeople in Bolivia, India, Nigeria, Japan, and Germany envisioned these systems' value in public safety and policing, corporate contexts, and social interactions to reduce crime, increase security, improve efficiency, and enhance convenience in respective processes. Similar to the results emerging from the discourses on genAI, people considered the envisioned values to be achievable only if certain requirements are met and particular measures implemented. These requirements include, among others, having robust, privacy-preserving systems that are built and deployed in accordance with regulatory frameworks. Participants also emphasized the relevance of involving stakeholders in several governance steps and establishing awareness of how the technology functions. The researchers observed that positive corporate and governmental narratives influenced people's positive perspectives. Despite expressing concerns about validity or inaccuracy, participants attributed abilities related to the above-described envisioned values to facial processing technology. The participants' suggestions for regulatory measures potentially mitigated their concerns.

Overall, the majority of participants demanded that AI systems be regulated. They also highlighted the importance of keeping societies, especially lay citizens, in the loop to discuss desirable AI development and deployment. This was deemed especially important when discussing the appropriate mechanisms for governing these technologies, while paying attention to local factors, such as prevailing narratives that influence perceptions, to help question technology narratives and technology deployment.

case_data.inclusion-efforts: With the aim of providing a space for laypeople across different countries to explore and express their opinions on desirable AI development and deployment, we decided on a mix of participant selection methods. The participant outreach process employed targeted recruitment through various digital and analog communication channels and engagement with communities (e.g., neighbourhood associations, …) that shared information about the dialogues. This approach aimed to enhance diversity in gender, age, and AI knowledge, resulting in a self-selected pre-registered set of the interested general population. We chose self-selection based on the principle of universality, which reflects a participatory ideal of citizen engagement. We implemented purposive sampling with a random component on all pre-registrations. We ensured that each dialogue workshop group was gender-diverse and diverse across age clusters (20-year intervals: ‘low’, ‘middle’, ‘high’) and AI knowledge levels (‘low’, ‘middle’, ‘high’). We refer to the group of laypeople selected through this approach as a “mini-public,” in which people gather to discuss matters of public interest.
case_data.submitted-by: Chiara Ullstein, Michel Hohendanner and Jens Grossklags.

As a multi-country research project, the Global AI Dialogues enable comparative analysis of the results. This analysis was performed by an international research team, composed of the researchers who organized and facilitated the local dialogues, through joint analysis workshops.
